metadata.title: Discovery of the key contextual factors relevant to the reading performance of elementary school students from 61 countries/regions: insight from a machine learning-based approach

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the PIRLS 2016 international database (61 countries/regions; fourth-grade students) and constructs a binary classification target based on PIRLS reading benchmarks (high >550 vs low <475). The manuscript describes preprocessing (deleting cases with >20% missingness, imputing remaining missing values with a nearest-neighbor mean, and normalizing features) and then trains an SVM with a linear kernel using LIBSVM in Python. No PIRLS sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) are reported or referenced in the methods, and the ML pipeline is described as a standard k-fold cross-validation procedure. Because SVMs do not natively incorporate complex survey weights, the analysis appears to be conducted without applying PIRLS complex-survey weights, which may limit population-representativeness and uncertainty quantification under the nested sampling design.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the PIRLS 2016 public international database for fourth-grade students from 61 participating countries/regions. Selected students based on reading benchmark thresholds: high-performing cohort defined as reading score above 550 and low-performing cohort defined as reading score below 475 (intermediate benchmark students between 475 and 550 are excluded). For preprocessing, cases with more than 20% missing data were deleted; remaining missing values were imputed using a nearest-neighbor mean approach; then features were centered and variance-scaled prior to SVM training.

main_findings.performance_metrics: SVM (linear kernel) with 5-fold cross-validation: Accuracy 81.94%, Sensitivity 73.00%, Specificity 87.97%, Precision 0.8036, AUC 0.8049. SVM–RFE–CV (optimal 20 factors): Accuracy 79.72%, Sensitivity 74.55%, Specificity 85.98%, Precision 0.7965, AUC 0.8015.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 Reading the study leveraged gender, reading motivation/attribution beliefs, and home literacy resources (e.g., children’s books at home) to classify students into high- vs low-performing reading cohorts, finding that the SVM achieved strong discrimination (AUC ≈ 0.805) and that an optimal set of 20 contextual factors retained nearly the same performance (AUC ≈ 0.802). This indicates that strengthening student motivation and home literacy environments—alongside addressing school-level instructional constraints—may improve the likelihood of reaching high reading benchmarks, though the results are descriptive/predictive and do not establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study extracted PIRLS 2016 fourth-grade reading data from 61 countries/regions (N=183,428) and defined a binary target using PIRLS benchmarks: high-performing students scored above 550, while low-performing students scored below 475 (intermediate students were excluded). For the dependent variable, the authors used a single plausible value (ASRREA01) to represent overall reading performance. They trained a linear-kernel SVM (LIBSVM) and evaluated it with fivefold cross-validation, reporting Accuracy 81.94% and AUC 0.8049 (Sensitivity 73.00%, Specificity 87.97%). Using SVM–RFE with cross-validation, they selected an optimal set of 20 contextual factors out of 106 and obtained Accuracy 79.72% and AUC 0.8015, indicating stable discrimination with fewer predictors. Missing data were handled by deleting cases with >20% missingness and imputing remaining missing values via a nearest-neighbor mean; however, the paper does not report applying PIRLS sampling/replicate weights, and the approach is exploratory/predictive rather than causal.
